rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast scouting gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs. The strong final solvent minimizes truncation risk, while the intermediate temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test whether selectivity changes separate the central cluster and late doublet. The short elution window leaves ample room for a shallower gradient afterward.

Halve the gradient slope at the more promising temperature to test whether the three unresolved pairs gain separation. The current last peak at 4.71 minutes gives room to spread the peaks without incurring a time penalty.

The shallower gradient nearly resolved everything, but the remaining close pair may need a selectivity shift rather than further stretching alone. Lower temperature by one step and extend the gradient modestly to preserve separation in the central cluster while targeting full resolution before 10 minutes.

Restore 60 C to recover central-cluster selectivity while retaining the shallower gradient. This tests whether the remaining R = 1.27 pair from injection 3 reaches full resolution with the last peak still below 10 minutes.

The late critical pair worsened when the gradient became shallower, whereas the central pairs improved. This slope lies just steeper than injection 3, targeting R ≥ 1.5 for both groups while keeping all peaks comfortably within 10 minutes.

Increase the slope slightly from 0.04444 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to lift the R = 1.49 pair above threshold while preserving the central separations. The gradient remains linear throughout the observed elution window, so the lower endpoint should not delay the last peak.

Injection 7 has reached the maximum CRF; now test a shorter elution window by raising the starting organic fraction one step while preserving gradient slope. Retain injection 7 as the fully resolved benchmark if the critical pairs lose resolution.

Slightly flatten the gradient to recover the central separations lost at the higher starting organic fraction. This tests whether full resolution can be restored with a last peak earlier than injection 7, which remains the maximum-score benchmark.

The higher-starting-organic trials expose competing critical pairs, so retain injection 7 as the maximum-score method. Test the low-temperature selectivity regime with a fast, broad gradient to look for a different route to a shorter fully resolved separation.

Keep the promising low-temperature selectivity and flatten the gradient one step to test improvement of the two unresolved pairs. The 6.06-minute last peak leaves room to gain resolution while potentially remaining faster than injection 7.

The low-temperature critical pairs respond oppositely to gradient duration. Raise the starting organic fraction while modestly reducing slope to test a different selectivity balance and shorten elution, retaining injection 7 as the proven maximum-score method.

Continue the higher-starting-organic trend at 25 C, which improved both critical pairs and shortened the last retention time in injection 12. This tests whether further narrowing the solvent window can achieve full resolution faster than the established maximum-score method.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to improve the remaining R = 1.43 late pair while testing whether the central pair retains its R = 1.62 separation. This could deliver full resolution with a substantially earlier last peak than injection 7.

Raise the starting organic fraction one grid step while preserving the successful gradient slope to seek earlier elution. Injection 14 remains the shortest fully resolved benchmark if this shift compromises any critical pair.
Flatten the gradient one step to improve the two deficient pairs at the higher starting organic fraction. This may restore full resolution while keeping the last peak earlier than injection 14.
Raise temperature one step from the shortest fully resolved method to test faster elution. Injection 16 provides a maximum-score fallback if the temperature shift reduces critical-pair selectivity.

Return to 25 C and test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to compensate for lost central-pair resolution. This explores a shorter fully resolved separation while retaining injection 16 as the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Bracket the fastest fully resolved slope at phi0 = 0.35 with a gradient midway between injections 15 and 16. This tests whether the critical central pair remains above 1.5 while reducing the last retention time below 4.14 minutes.

Test whether a further increase in starting organic fraction moves the central critical pair through its selectivity crossover into a faster resolved regime. Flatten the gradient at phi0 = 0.40 to test whether the central pair can recover full resolution before the longer gradient offsets the time saved by the higher starting organic fraction. Keep injection 16 as the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method.

Refine around injection 16 with a slightly shallower gradient to increase the resolution margin of its critical pairs. The maximum CRF is already secured; this trial targets a less borderline fully resolved method with all peaks still eluting well before 10 minutes.

Test whether a larger temperature shift moves the central pair past its selectivity crossover into a faster resolved regime. Injection 16 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method, while this trial checks an unexplored temperature region.

Shorten the programmed gradient while preserving injection 16’s starting composition and slope throughout its observed elution window. This should retain maximum CRF and the approximately 4.14-minute last peak while avoiding an unnecessarily high final organic fraction.

Shorten the programmed gradient to four minutes while preserving the slope of the fastest proven fully resolved method. The gradient ends at the outlet at 4.65 minutes, after the observed last peak at 4.14 minutes, so this should preserve maximum CRF with a lower final organic fraction.
